metadata.dcterms:title: The Effectiveness of Business Process Visualisations: a Systematic Literature Review
metadata.dcterms:creator: [0000-0002-4210-2342], Ed Overes1
Santoro2[0000-0003-3421-1894], Flavia Maria
metadata.dcterms:abstract: Business Process Visualisations (BPVs) have become indispensable tools for organisations seeking to enhance their operational efficiency, decision-making capabilities, and overall performance. The burgeoning interest in process modeling and tool development, coupled with the rise of data visualisation field, underscores the significant role of visual tools in leveraging human cognition. Unlike traditional models, data visualisation approaches graphics from a novel angle, emphasising the potency of visual representations. This review aims to integrate the domains of BPV and data visualisation to assess their combined influence on organisational effectiveness comprehensively. Through a meticulous analysis of existing literature, this study aims to amalgamate insights on BPVs impact from a data visualisation standpoint, advocating for a design philosophy that prioritises user engagement to bolster organisational outcomes. Additionally, our systematic review has unveiled promising avenues for future research, identifying underexplored variables that influence the efficacy of BPVs, thereby charting a path for forthcoming scholarly inquiries.

metadata.dcterms:title: Introduction to the Analysis of Probabilistic Decision-Making Algorithms
metadata.dcterms:creator: Algorithms, Decision-Making
metadata.dcterms:abstract: Decision theories offer principled methods for making choices under various types of uncertainty. Algorithms that implement these theories have been success- fully applied to a wide range of real-world problems, including materials and drug discovery. Indeed, they are desirable since they can adaptively gather information to make better decisions in the future, resulting in data-efficient workflows. In scien- tific discovery, where experiments are costly, these algorithms can thus significantly reduce the cost of experimentation. Theoretical analyses of these algorithms are cru- cial for understanding their behavior and providing valuable insights for developing next-generation algorithms. However, theoretical analyses in the literature are often inaccessible to non-experts. This monograph aims to provide an accessible, self- contained introduction to the theoretical analysis of commonly used probabilistic decision-making algorithms, including bandit algorithms, Bayesian optimization, and tree search algorithms. Only basic knowledge of probability theory and statis- tics, along with some elementary knowledge about Gaussian processes, is assumed. arXiv:2508.21620v2 [cs.LG] 23 May 2026

metadata.dcterms:creator: Calvanese1, Diego
Dumas2, Marlon
Laurson2, Ülari
metadata.dcterms:abstract: The Decision Model and Notation (DMN) is a standard no- tation to capture decision logic in business applications in general and business processes in particular. A central construct in DMN is that of a decision table. The increasing use of DMN decision tables to capture critical business knowledge raises the need to support analysis tasks on these tables such as correctness and completeness checking. This paper provides a formal semantics for DMN tables, a formal deﬁnition of key analysis tasks and scalable algorithms to tackle two such tasks, i.e., de- tection of overlapping rules and of missing rules. The algorithms are based on a geometric interpretation of decision tables that can be used to support other analysis tasks by tapping into geometric algorithms. The algorithms have been implemented in an open-source DMN editor and tested on large decision tables derived from a credit lending dataset.

metadata.dcterms:title: Defending Against Prompt Injection With a Few DefensiveTokens
metadata.dcterms:creator: Chen, Sizhe
metadata.dcterms:abstract: When large language model (LLM) systems interact with exter- nal data to perform complex tasks, a new attack, namely prompt injection, becomes a significant threat. By injecting instructions into the data accessed by the system, the attacker is able to over- ride the initial user task with an arbitrary task directed by the attacker. To secure the system, test-time defenses, e.g., defensive prompting, have been proposed for system developers to attain security only when needed in a flexible manner. However, they are much less effective than training-time defenses that change the model parameters. Motivated by this, we propose DefensiveToken, a test-time defense with prompt injection robustness comparable to training-time alternatives. DefensiveTokens are newly inserted as special tokens, whose embeddings are optimized for security. In security-sensitive cases, system developers can append a few DefensiveTokens before the LLM input to achieve security with a minimal utility drop. In scenarios where security is less of a con- cern, developers can simply skip DefensiveTokens; the LLM system remains the same as there is no defense, generating high-quality responses. Thus, DefensiveTokens, if released alongside the model, allow a flexible switch between the state-of-the-art (SOTA) utility and almost-SOTA security at test time. The code is available here. metadata.dcterms:title: A Skill-Based Agentic Pipeline for Library of Congress Subject Indexing
metadata.dcterms:creator: Chow, Eric H. C.
metadata.dcterms:abstract: This paper presents a modular AI agentic skill pipeline for au- tomating subject indexing with Library of Congress Subject Headings (LCSH). Subject indexing—the process of analyzing a work’s aboutness, selecting controlled vocabulary terms, and encoding them as MARC 21 subject access fields—is one of the most time-consuming components of library cataloging. The system decomposes this process into four discrete, sequentially executed agent skills: conceptual analysis, quantitative filtering, authority validation, and MARC field synthesis. Each skill encodes domain knowledge drawn directly from Library of Congress Subject Headings Manual (SHM) instruction sheets and subject analysis theory. The pipeline was evaluated against a corpus of ten titles whose existing subject headings were captured from the Harvard Library bibliographic dataset (a snapshot of their Alma ILS). Results demonstrate strong con- ceptual alignment with professional subject indexing practice, with notable differences in specificity, subdivision practice, and the agent’s adherence to the 2026 LC policy discontinuing form subdivisions ($v) in favor of LCGFT 655 fields.

metadata.dcterms:title: Authoring Agent Skills: A Software-Engineering Approach
metadata.dcterms:creator: Destefanis, Giuseppe
metadata.dcterms:abstract: Agent Skills are an emerging way to extend large language model agents with reusable procedural knowledge that the agent loads on demand. Anthropic introduced Agent Skills and published the format as an open specification supported across several agent tools. This note argues that a skill is a software artefact and that its construction should follow software-engineering principles, with qualifications: single responsibility, separation of interface from implementation, low coupling, and economy in a shared token budget, together with behavioural evaluation in place of deterministic testing. Using Claude Code as the reference implementation, it describes how a skill is structured, how its contents are loaded in stages, and how to write the description on which selection depends. It places skills against the other mechanisms a developer can use to shape agent behaviour, like project memory files, slash commands, subagents, external tool connections, and hooks, and gives a rule for choosing between them based on who decides that a mechanism runs and what guarantee it provides. It then sets out an evaluation-driven authoring process, a set of patterns and faults commonly encountered in authoring, and the trust question raised by using skills from third parties. We illustrate the comparison drawn in UML class style, the loading model, the anatomy of a skill, the relative position of each mechanism, and the points at which skills and hooks act during a session. Note on sources This note draws on Anthropic’s official documentation1 for Agent Skills, Claude Code skills, hooks, and skill authoring best practices, together with the open Agent Skills specification.

metadata.dcterms:title: Doc-Researcher: A Unified System for Multimodal Document Parsing and Deep Research

Zhang, Zhi

metadata.dcterms:abstract: Deep Research systems have revolutionized how LLMs solve com- plex questions through iterative reasoning and evidence gathering. However, current systems remain fundamentally constrained to textual web data, overlooking the vast knowledge embedded in mul- timodal documents: scientific papers, technical reports, and finan- cial documents where critical information exists in figures, tables, charts, and equations. Processing such documents demands sophis- ticated parsing to preserve visual semantics, intelligent chunking to maintain structural coherence, and adaptive retrieval across modal- ities, which are capabilities absent in existing systems. In response, we present Doc-Researcher, a unified system that bridges this gap through three integrated components: (i) deep multimodal parsing that preserves layout structure and visual semantics while creating multi-granular representations from chunk to document level, (ii) systematic retrieval architecture supporting text-only, vision-only, and hybrid paradigms with dynamic granularity selec- tion, and (iii) iterative multi-agent workflows that decompose complex queries, progressively accumulate evidence, and synthesize comprehensive answers across documents and modalities. To enable rigorous evaluation, we introduce M4DocBench, the first bench- mark for Multi-modal, Multi-hop, Multi-document, and Multi-turn deep research. Featuring 158 expert-annotated questions with com- plete evidence chains across 304 documents, M4DocBench tests capabilities that existing benchmarks cannot assess. Experiments demonstrate that Doc-Researcher achieves 50.6% accuracy, 3.4× better than state-of-the-art baselines, validating that effective docu- ment research requires not just better retrieval, but fundamentally deep parsing that preserve multimodal integrity and support itera- tive research. Our work establishes a new paradigm for conducting deep research on multimodal document collections. CCS Concepts • Information systems →Multimodal

metadata.dcterms:title: Debiased Inference for AI-Generated Data without Gold-Standard Labels: Identification via Multiple Imperfect Measurements
metadata.dcterms:creator: Egami†, Naoki
metadata.dcterms:abstract: An increasing number of scholars use AI to measure variables they subsequently include in downstream analyses. Although AI-measured variables are often analyzed as if observed without error, ignoring prediction errors in automated measurement leads to substantial bias and invalid confidence intervals in downstream analyses, even if AI measurement accuracy is high, e.g., above 90%. Existing solutions, such as design-based supervised learning and prediction-powered infer- ence, combine error-prone AI-based measurements with gold-standard labels, which may be costly and difficult to obtain in some application areas. In this paper, we propose debiased inference with multiple imperfect measurements (DMM), a framework that combines multiple error-prone AI measurements to enable valid downstream inference without gold-standard labels. Building on the established results on CP decomposition, DMM assumes that these measurements are independent conditional on the latent true label and observed unit-level features, such as text features represented by embeddings. This framework allows for unknown misclassification rates to vary across annotation methods (e.g., large language models) and across units of annotation (e.g., texts). Under this assumption, we use semiparamet- ric inference theory to prove that the DMM estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal, enabling valid inference for a wide range of downstream statistical analyses common in the so- cial sciences. Our simulation results show that DMM yields valid inference and that adding accurate, though imperfect, measurements can improve efficiency. metadata.dcterms:title: Lightweight Compositional Embeddings for Incremental Streaming Recommendation
metadata.dcterms:creator: Hang1, Mengyue
Schnabel2, Tobias
Yang2, Longqi
Neville1, Jennifer
metadata.dcterms:abstract: Most work in graph-based recommender systems considers a static setting where all information about test nodes (i.e., users and items) is available upfront at training time. However, this static setting makes little sense for many real world applications where data comes in continuously as a stream of new edges and nodes, and one has to update model predictions incrementally to reflect the latest state. To fully capitalize on the newly available data in the stream, recent graph-based recommendation models would need to be repeatedly retrained, which is infeasible in practice. In this pa- per, we study the graph-based streaming recommendation setting and propose a compositional recommendation model—Lightweight Compositional Embedding (LCE)—that supports incremental up- dates under low computational cost. Instead of learning explicit embeddings for the full set of nodes, LCE learns explicit embed- dings for only a subset of nodes and represents the other nodes implicitly, through a composition function based on their interac- tions in the graph. This provides an effective, yet efficient, means to leverage streaming graph data when one node type (e.g., items) is more amenable to static representation. We conduct an extensive empirical study to compare LCE to a set of competitive baselines on three large-scale user-item recommendation datasets with inter- actions under a streaming setting. The results demonstrate the su- perior performance of LCE, showing that it achieves nearly skyline performance with significantly fewer parameters than alternative graph-based models.

metadata.dcterms:abstract: Advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have led to significant interest in their potential to support human experts across a range of domains, including public health. In this work we present automated evaluations of LLMs for public health tasks involving the classification and extraction of free text. We combine six externally annotated datasets with seven new internally annotated datasets to evaluate LLMs for processing text related to: health burden, epidemiological risk factors, and public health interventions. We evaluate eleven open-weight LLMs (7-123 billion parameters) across all tasks using zero-shot in-context learning. We find that Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct is the highest performing model, achieving the best results on 8/16 tasks (using micro-F1 scores). We see significant variation across tasks with all open-weight LLMs scoring below 60% micro-F1 on some challenging tasks, such as Contact Classification, while all LLMs achieve greater than 80% micro-F1 on others, such as GI Illness Classification. For a subset of 11 tasks, we also evaluate three GPT-4 and GPT-4o series models and find comparable results to Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct. Overall, based on these initial results we find promising signs that LLMs may be useful tools for public health experts to extract information from a wide variety of free text sources, and support public health surveillance, research, and interventions. metadata.dcterms:title: Improving information retrieval through correspondence analysis instead of latent semantic analysis
metadata.dcterms:abstract: The initial dimensions extracted by latent semantic analysis (LSA) of a document-term matrix have been shown to mainly display marginal effects, which are irrelevant for information retrieval. To improve the performance of LSA, usually the elements of the raw document- term matrix are weighted and the weighting exponent of singular values can be adjusted. An alternative information retrieval technique that ignores the marginal effects is correspon- dence analysis (CA). In this paper, the information retrieval performance of LSA and CA is empirically compared. Moreover, it is explored whether the two weightings also improve the performance of CA. The results for four empirical datasets show that CA always performs better than LSA. Weighting the elements of the raw data matrix can improve CA; however, it is data dependent and the improvement is small. Adjusting the singular value weighting exponent often improves the performance of CA; however, the extent of the improvement depends on the dataset and the number of dimensions.

metadata.dcterms:abstract: Model-Driven Engineering (MDE) places models at the core of system and data engineering processes. In the context of research data, these models are typically expressed as schemas that define the structure and semantics of datasets. However, many domains still lack standardized models, and creating them remains a significant barrier, especially for non- experts. We present a hybrid approach that combines large language models (LLMs) with deterministic techniques to enable JSON Schema creation, modification, and schema mapping based on natural language inputs by the user. These capabilities are integrated into the open-source tool MetaConfigurator, which already provides visual model editing, validation, code gener- ation, and form generation from models. For data integration, we generate schema mappings from heterogeneous JSON, CSV, XML, and YAML data using LLMs, while ensuring scalability and reliability through deterministic execution of generated mapping rules. The applicability of our work is demonstrated in an application example in the field of chemistry. By combining natural language interaction with deterministic safeguards, this work significantly lowers the barrier to structured data modeling and data integration for non-experts. Our study advances understanding by examining the detailed representation features of decision models, including type (tree versus table), structure (expanded versus frugal), and design (monochromatic versus colored). We demonstrate that the use of color can improve model-task fit, and that structural features can enhance comprehension. Utilizing eye-tracking, we analyzed the underlying mechanisms of these effects. Our findings provide valuable insights for cognitive information systems research and practical applications, offering guidance for both users and developers of decision models.

metadata.dcterms:abstract: Background: Pneumococcal disease caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae results in considerable mortality and morbidity. Pneumococcal conjugate vaccines (PCV), such as PCV-13, can prevent invasive pneumococcal disease and avoid disability and death. The cost of introducing PCV-13 in childhood immunization schedules should be assessed against the cost of pneumococcal diseases for each community. Aims: This study aimed to evaluate the cost–effectiveness of introducing PCV-13 in the national immunization programme for children under 5 years in the Islamic Republic of Iran. Methods: The TRIVAC decision support model was used to estimate total costs of introducing PCV-13 and the disability-adjusted life years (DALYs)averted. The main pneumococcal diseases were considered—pneumonia, meningitis, acute otitis media, and non-pneumonia, non-meningitis infections—in terms of hospital admissions, outpatient visits and deaths. Local data were used to estimate costs. Results: Pneumococcal disease is estimated to affect 18 713 211 children under 5 years (519 412 pneumonia, 18 148 116 acute otitis media, 6884 meningitis, and 38 799 non-pneumonia, non-meningitis)in 10 years (2014–2023)without use of the vaccine. Introduction of PCV-13 would prevent 4 900 084 cases of pneumococcal disease (190 849 pneumonia, 4 692 450 acute otitis media, 2529 meningitis, and 14 256 non-pneumonia, non-meningitis). Pneumococcal infection would cause 287 950 hospital admissions and 29 399 deaths; vaccination could avert 105 802 hospital admissions and 9997 deaths. The incremental cost–effectiveness was estimated to be US$ 1890 and US$ 1538 per averted DALY for the government and society respectively. Conclusion: According to WHO-recommended thresholds for interpreting cost–effectiveness, introduction of PCV-13 for children under 5 years in the Islamic Republic of Iran would be cost-effective

metadata.dcterms:title: Healthy LLMs? Benchmarking LLM Knowledge of UK Government Public Health Information
metadata.dcterms:creator: KNOWL-, BENCHMARKING LLM
metadata.dcterms:abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) become widely accessible, a detailed un- derstanding of their knowledge within specific domains becomes necessary for successful real world use. This is particularly critical in the domains of medicine and public health, where failure to retrieve relevant, accurate, and current infor- mation could significantly impact UK residents. However, while there are a num- ber of LLM benchmarks in the medical domain, currently little is known about LLM knowledge within the field of public health. To address this issue, this pa- per introduces a new benchmark, PubHealthBench, with over 8000 questions for evaluating LLMs’ Multiple Choice Question Answering (MCQA) and free form responses to public health queries. To create PubHealthBench we extract free text from 687 current UK government guidance documents and implement an automated pipeline for generating MCQA samples. Assessing 24 LLMs on Pub- HealthBench we find the latest proprietary LLMs (GPT-4.5, GPT-4.1 and o1) have a high degree of knowledge, achieving over 90% accuracy in the MCQA setup, and outperform humans with cursory search engine use. However, in the free form setup we see lower performance with no model scoring over 75%. There- fore, while there are promising signs that state of the art (SOTA) LLMs are an increasingly accurate source of public health information, additional safeguards or tools may still be needed when providing free form responses. metadata.dcterms:creator: Li†, Han
metadata.dcterms:abstract: Issue resolution has made remarkable progress thanks to the ad- vanced reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). Recently, agent-based frameworks such as SWE-agent have further advanced this progress by enabling autonomous, tool-using agents to tackle complex software engineering tasks. While existing agent- based issue resolution approaches are primarily based on agents’ independent explorations, they often get stuck in local solutions and fail to identify issue patterns that span across different parts of the codebase. To address this limitation, we propose SWE-Debate, a competitive multi-agent debate framework that encourages diverse reasoning paths and achieves more consolidated issue localization. SWE-Debate first creates multiple fault propagation traces as local- ization proposals by traversing a code dependency graph. Then, it organizes a three-round debate among specialized agents, each em- bodying distinct reasoning perspectives along the fault propagation trace. This structured competition enables agents to collaboratively converge on a consolidated fix plan. Finally, this consolidated fix plan is integrated into an MCTS-based code modification agent for patch generation. Experiments on the SWE-bench benchmark show that SWE-Debate achieves new state-of-the-art results in open-source agent frameworks and outperforms baselines by a large margin1.

metadata.dcterms:title: The Metanym Game: An LLM Benchmark Without Ground Truth That Rises With the Models It Measures
metadata.dcterms:creator: MEASURES, IT
metadata.dcterms:abstract: We introduce a benchmark that is fully self-contained, needs no ground truth, and rises with the models it measures. Language models compete at making analo- gies and subjectively grade one another; nothing enters from outside. The bench- mark reproduces GPQA Diamond, a keyed benchmark of expert-written ques- tions, at r = 0.98, audited for a leak and found clean. We hypothesize that both benchmarks measure the same thing in different ways: a language model holds its knowledge as archetypal contexts, relationship patterns valid across many topic domains. GPQA instantiates the required knowledge in one domain; the Metanym Game instantiates one archetype into several domains, generating analogies, no reasoning required. The reasoning feature of an LLM hardly changes the game’s ratings, while it lifts GPQA, which requires derivations. In the game, a player writes a context template whose slots, filled with a set of keywords from a topic domain, instantiate a factually true description of that domain; the instantiations are each other’s metaphors, and keywords filling the same slot are metanyms, metaphorically synonymous. Correctness is settled sentence by sentence. Ground truth is replaced by the SVD of the factual rating matrix: its left and right singular vectors rate the players as judges and as generators, two ratings from one factori- sation, to our knowledge a first for an LLM council of peers. On the subjective criteria, judges are weighted by their rating consistency under a swept calibration anchor. Generating and judging are different skills: on this roster the strongest generators were middling judges. A council of the five best issues the official ratings; its contestable seats keep it current, a candidate steering signal for self- improving AI. The paper is accompanied by a validating package that recomputes every number.

metadata.dcterms:title: TCAndon-Router: Adaptive Reasoning Router for Multi-Agent Collaboration
metadata.dcterms:creator: Multi-Agent Collaboration
metadata.dcterms:abstract: Multi-Agent Systems(MAS) have become a powerful paradigm for building high performance intelli- gent applications. Within these systems, the router responsible for determining which expert agents should handle a given query plays a crucial role in overall performance. Existing routing strategies generally fall into two categories: performance routing, which balances latency and cost across mod- els of different sizes, and task routing, which assigns queries to domain-specific experts to improve accuracy. In real-world enterprise applications, task routing is more suitable; however, most existing approaches rely on static single-label decisions, which introduce two major limitations: (i) diﬀiculty in seamlessly integrating new agents as business domains expand, and (ii) routing conflicts caused by overlapping agent capabilities, ultimately degrading accuracy and robustness.To address these challenges, we propose TCAndon-Router(TCAR): an adaptive reasoning router for multi-agent col- laboration. Unlike traditional routers, TCAR supports dynamic agent onboarding and first generates a natural-language reasoning chain before predicting a set of candidate agents capable of handling the query. In addition, we design a collaborative execution pipeline in which selected agents indepen- dently produce responses, which are then aggregated and refined into a single high-quality response by a dedicated Refining Agent.Experiments on public datasets and real enterprise data demonstrate that TCAR significantly improves routing accuracy, reduces routing conflicts, and remains robust in am- biguous scenarios. We have released TCAR at https://huggingface.co/tencent/TCAndon-Router to support future research on explainable and collaborative multi-agent routing.

metadata.dcterms:title: Stratégie mondiale pour la santé numérique 2020-2025
metadata.dcterms:creator: Organisation mondiale de la Santé
metadata.dcterms:abstract:
La Stratégie mondiale pour la santé numérique 2020–2025 fournit un cadre destiné à aider les États Membres à renforcer leurs systèmes de santé grâce à l’adoption et à l’utilisation appropriées des technologies numériques. Élaborée en réponse aux mandats de l’Assemblée mondiale de la Santé et alignée sur les Objectifs de développement durable ainsi que sur les objectifs du « Triple milliard » de l’OMS, cette stratégie présente une vision commune visant à améliorer la santé et le bien-être au moyen de solutions de santé numérique accessibles, abordables, sûres et durables. Elle souligne l’importance d’une gouvernance solide, de l’interopérabilité, de l’utilisation éthique des données, de la protection de la vie privée, du renforcement des capacités des personnels de santé et des investissements dans les infrastructures numériques afin de soutenir les priorités nationales de santé et la couverture sanitaire universelle.
Le document définit quatre objectifs stratégiques : promouvoir la collaboration mondiale et le partage des connaissances ; faire progresser la mise en œuvre des stratégies nationales de santé numérique ; renforcer la gouvernance de la santé numérique aux niveaux mondial, régional et national ; et promouvoir des systèmes de santé centrés sur les personnes grâce aux technologies numériques. Il présente également des principes directeurs, un cadre de mise en œuvre et des mécanismes de suivi destinés à soutenir les pays dans le développement d’écosystèmes numériques interopérables. Une attention particulière est accordée aux obstacles rencontrés par les pays à revenu faible ou intermédiaire et à la nécessité de veiller à ce que la transformation numérique contribue à des systèmes de santé plus équitables, efficaces et résilients.

metadata.dcterms:title: Lignes directrices de l'OMS : recommandations sur les interventions numériques pour le renforcement des systèmes de santé
metadata.dcterms:creator: Organisation mondiale de la Santé
metadata.dcterms:abstract:
Ces lignes directrices de l’OMS présentent des recommandations fondées sur des données probantes concernant l’utilisation des interventions numériques pour renforcer les systèmes de santé et soutenir les progrès vers la couverture sanitaire universelle (CSU). Élaborées en réponse à l’adoption croissante des technologies numériques et à la résolution sur la santé numérique approuvée par l’Assemblée mondiale de la Santé en 2018, elles répondent à la nécessité d’évaluer rigoureusement les interventions de santé numérique afin que les investissements reposent sur des données probantes relatives à leurs avantages, leurs inconvénients, leur acceptabilité, leur faisabilité, leurs implications en matière de ressources et les considérations d’équité. Les lignes directrices soulignent que les technologies numériques doivent compléter, et non remplacer, les composantes fondamentales de systèmes de santé performants.
Les recommandations portent sur un ensemble prioritaire d’interventions de santé numérique, principalement accessibles au moyen d’appareils mobiles, notamment la notification des naissances et des décès, la notification des stocks et la gestion des produits de base, la télémédecine entre client et prestataire ainsi qu’entre prestataires, la communication ciblée avec les clients, le suivi numérique de l’état de santé et des services reçus, les outils d’aide à la décision destinés aux professionnels de santé et l’apprentissage numérique. Les lignes directrices présentent également des considérations relatives à la mise en œuvre, recensent les principales lacunes en matière de recherche et visent à aider les ministères de la santé, les responsables des politiques de santé, les professionnels de santé, les partenaires du développement et les autres parties prenantes à prendre des décisions éclairées concernant l’adoption, le déploiement à grande échelle et l’institutionnalisation des interventions de santé numérique efficaces.

metadata.dcterms:title: Classification des interventions, des services et des applications numériques dans le domaine de la santé : un langage commun pour décrire les diverses utilisations de la technologie numérique dans le domaine de la santé
metadata.dcterms:creator: Organisation mondiale de la Santé
metadata.dcterms:abstract:
Cette deuxième édition de la Classification des interventions, services et applications numériques en santé présente une taxonomie normalisée permettant de décrire la manière dont les technologies numériques sont utilisées pour répondre aux besoins des individus et des systèmes de santé. Élaborée par l’OMS, cette classification établit un langage commun destiné à faciliter la communication entre les décideurs, les responsables de programmes de santé, les chercheurs, les responsables de mise en œuvre, les développeurs de technologies et les autres acteurs du domaine de la santé numérique. Elle organise les interventions numériques en santé autour de capacités technologiques distinctes conçues pour répondre à des défis des systèmes de santé et relie ces interventions aux services et types d’applications numériques qui les mettent en œuvre.
La publication met à jour et élargit la première édition publiée en 2018 afin de refléter les progrès des technologies de santé numérique, l’évolution des pratiques de mise en œuvre et les enseignements tirés de leur utilisation à l’échelle mondiale. Le cadre est structuré autour de trois axes interconnectés : les défis des systèmes de santé, les interventions numériques en santé et les services et types d’applications numériques. Il comprend des interventions destinées aux personnes, aux prestataires de soins, aux gestionnaires des systèmes de santé et aux services de données, ainsi que des catégories d’applications numériques et de systèmes d’information. Cette classification vise à soutenir la planification, la mise en œuvre, l’analyse des investissements, la recherche, l’interopérabilité, l’élaboration des politiques et la gouvernance des initiatives de santé numérique.

La Estrategia mundial sobre salud digital 2020–2025 proporciona un marco para apoyar a los Estados Miembros en el fortalecimiento de los sistemas de salud mediante la adopción y el uso adecuados de las tecnologías digitales. Elaborada en respuesta a los mandatos de la Asamblea Mundial de la Salud y alineada con los Objetivos de Desarrollo Sostenible y las metas de los “Tres Mil Millones” de la OMS, la estrategia establece una visión compartida para mejorar la salud y el bienestar a través de soluciones de salud digital accesibles, asequibles, seguras y sostenibles. Destaca la importancia de una gobernanza sólida, la interoperabilidad, el uso ético de los datos, la protección de la privacidad, el fortalecimiento de las capacidades del personal sanitario y la inversión en infraestructura digital para apoyar las prioridades nacionales de salud y la cobertura sanitaria universal.
El documento define cuatro objetivos estratégicos: promover la colaboración mundial y el intercambio de conocimientos; avanzar en la implementación de estrategias nacionales de salud digital; fortalecer la gobernanza de la salud digital a nivel mundial, regional y nacional; y fomentar sistemas de salud centrados en las personas mediante el uso de tecnologías digitales. Asimismo, presenta principios rectores, un marco de implementación y mecanismos de seguimiento destinados a apoyar a los países en el desarrollo de ecosistemas de salud digital interoperables. Se presta especial atención a los obstáculos que enfrentan los países de ingresos bajos y medianos y a garantizar que la transformación digital contribuya a sistemas de salud más equitativos, eficaces y resilientes.

metadata.dcterms:abstract:
Este documento presenta las recomendaciones de la OMS, basadas en la evidencia, sobre el uso de intervenciones digitales para fortalecer los sistemas de salud y apoyar el avance hacia la cobertura sanitaria universal (CSU). Elaborada en respuesta a la creciente adopción de las tecnologías digitales y a la resolución sobre salud digital aprobada por la Asamblea Mundial de la Salud en 2018, la directriz aborda la necesidad de evaluar rigurosamente las intervenciones de salud digital para garantizar que las inversiones se fundamenten en evidencia sobre sus beneficios, riesgos, aceptabilidad, factibilidad, implicaciones en materia de recursos y consideraciones de equidad. Asimismo, subraya que las tecnologías digitales deben complementar, y no sustituir, los componentes fundamentales de unos sistemas de salud sólidos y eficaces.
Las recomendaciones se centran en un conjunto priorizado de intervenciones de salud digital accesibles, como mínimo, mediante dispositivos móviles, entre ellas la notificación de nacimientos y defunciones, la notificación de existencias y la gestión de suministros, la telemedicina entre pacientes y profesionales y entre profesionales, la comunicación dirigida a los pacientes, el seguimiento digital del estado de salud y de los servicios recibidos, las herramientas de apoyo a la toma de decisiones para el personal sanitario y el aprendizaje digital para los trabajadores de la salud. La directriz también presenta consideraciones para la implementación, identifica las principales lagunas de investigación y proporciona orientación a los ministerios de salud, los responsables de salud pública, los asociados para el desarrollo y otras partes interesadas para adoptar, ampliar e institucionalizar intervenciones de salud digital eficaces sobre la base de la mejor evidencia disponible.

La clasificación está concebida para apoyar la planificación, la implementación, el análisis de inversiones, la investigación, las consideraciones de interoperabilidad, la elaboración de políticas y la gobernanza de las iniciativas de salud digital, facilitando así un uso más coherente y eficaz de las tecnologías digitales en los sistemas de salud.

metadata.dcterms:title: Evaluating Model Explanations without Ground Truth
metadata.dcterms:creator: Rawal, Kaivalya
metadata.dcterms:abstract: There can be many competing and contradictory explanations for a single model prediction, making it difficult to select which one to use. Current explanation evaluation frameworks measure qual- ity by comparing against ideal “ground-truth” explanations, or by verifying model sensitivity to important inputs. We outline the limitations of these approaches, and propose three desirable princi- ples to ground the future development of explanation evaluation strategies for local feature importance explanations. We propose a ground-truth Agnostic eXplanation Evaluation framework (AXE) for evaluating and comparing model explanations that satis- fies these principles. Unlike prior approaches, AXE does not require access to ideal ground-truth explanations for comparison, or rely on model sensitivity – providing an independent measure of expla- nation quality. We verify AXE by comparing with baselines, and show how it can be used to detect explanation fairwashing. Our code is available at https://github.com/KaiRawal/Evaluating-Model- Explanations-without-Ground-Truth. CCS Concepts • Computing methodologies →Artificial intelligence; Ma- chine learning.

metadata.dcterms:title: SWE-Router: Routing in Multi-turn Agentic Software Engineering Tasks
metadata.dcterms:creator: Son, Seongho
Yoon, Sangwoong
Tang, Jiahua
Wang, Shuhan
Wolf, Lorenz
Bogunovic, Ilija
metadata.dcterms:abstract: Large language models (LLMs) embedded in multi-turn agentic harnesses are reshaping soft- ware engineering (SWE), but routing every task to a frontier model is wasteful when many issues admit cheap fixes. Existing LLM routers operate on the task description alone, which inherits an information-theoretic Bayes-error floor in agentic settings: a similar issue can hide either a localized typo or a multi-module refactor, and the prompt does not separate the two. We introduce SWE- Router, a value-based temporal approach that lets a cheap model run for a few exploratory turns and reads the resulting partial trajectory before de- ciding whether to continue cheaply or to escalate to an expensive model. We provide a Bayes- optimality theorem showing that conditioning on the partial trajectory never harms routing and is strictly better whenever exploration is informative. Across the LLM pairs of weak and strong models spanning the contemporary cost–capability frontier, we show that SWE-Router greatly improves the cost efficiency of SWE tasks, while maintaining the majority of the performances of the stronger model. We additionally release a multi-LLM trajectory dataset which allows reproduction of our trajectory-level routing.

metadata.dcterms:title: Annif at SemEval-2025 Task 5: Traditional XMTC augmented by LLMs
metadata.dcterms:creator: Suominen, Osma
Inkinen, Juho
Lehtinen, Mona
metadata.dcterms:abstract: This paper presents the Annif system in SemEval-2025 Task 5 (LLMs4Subjects), which focussed on subject indexing using large lan- guage models (LLMs). The task required creating subject predictions for bibliographic records from the bilingual TIBKAT database using the GND subject vocabulary. Our ap- proach combines traditional natural language processing and machine learning techniques im- plemented in the Annif toolkit with innovative LLM-based methods for translation and syn- thetic data generation, and merging predictions from monolingual models. The system ranked first in the all-subjects category and second in the tib-core-subjects category in the quantita- tive evaluation, and fourth in qualitative evalu- ations. These findings demonstrate the poten- tial of combining traditional XMTC algorithms with modern LLM techniques to improve the accuracy and efficiency of subject indexing in multilingual contexts.

metadata.dcterms:title: LCSHBench: A Multilingual, Consensus-Grounded Benchmark for Library of Congress Subject Heading Assignment
metadata.dcterms:creator: Tang, Kwok Leong
metadata.dcterms:abstract: Automated subject cataloging assigns controlled- vocabulary headings to bibliographic records, but LCSH has no standard public benchmark. We intro- duce LCSHBench: 22,346 books in 15 languages from the openly licensed Harvard, Columbia, and Prince- ton catalogs. Records enter only when at least two independent cataloging agencies assigned LCSH; we release per-catalog provenance plus union and unani- mous answer views. A concordance study of 465,187 works cataloged by all three libraries shows why this design matters: libraries usually agree on the under- lying topic (93.3% share a concept-level heading) but often differ in exact expression (39.4% have identical heading sets). LCSHBench therefore scores both ex- act and concept matches, with set and rank metrics broken down by language and heading type, across open-vocabulary generation and full-vocabulary re- trieval. As a first demonstration, a low-rank fine-tune of a 300M on-device embedder improves cross-lingual retrieval and beats a 3,072-dimensional hosted em- bedder on development exact recall@200 (0.659 vs 0.623). The language panel shows the gain is not uni- form, and held-out-test and end-to-end confirmation remain future work.

metadata.dcterms:title: CodeAgent : Autonomous Communicative Agents for Code Review
metadata.dcterms:creator: Tang1, Xunzhu
Kim2, Kisub
Song1, Yewei
Lothritz3, Cedric
Li4, Bei
Ezzini5, Saad
metadata.dcterms:abstract: Code review, which aims at ensuring the over- all quality and reliability of software, is a cor- nerstone of software development. Unfortu- nately, while crucial, Code review is a labor- intensive process that the research community is looking to automate. Existing automated methods rely on single input-output generative models and thus generally struggle to emulate the collaborative nature of code review. This work introduces CodeAgent, a novel multi- agent Large Language Model (LLM) system for code review automation. CodeAgent in- corporates a supervisory agent, QA-Checker, to ensure that all the agents’ contributions ad- dress the initial review question. We evaluated CodeAgent on critical code review tasks: (1) detect inconsistencies between code changes and commit messages, (2) identify vulnerabil- ity introductions, (3) validate code style ad- herence, and (4) suggest code revision. The results demonstrate CodeAgent’s effective- ness, contributing to a new state-of-the-art in code review automation. Our data and code are publicly available (https://github. com/Code4Agent/codeagent).

metadata.dcterms:creator: Tekanlou1, Hadi Bayrami Asl
Razmara1, Jafar
Sanaei1, Mahsa
metadata.dcterms:abstract: This paper presents our system, Homa, for SemEval-2025 Task 5: Subject Tagging, which focuses on automatically assigning subject la- bels to technical records from TIBKAT us- ing the Gemeinsame Normdatei (GND) tax- onomy. We leverage OntoAligner, a modu- lar ontology alignment toolkit, to address this task by integrating retrieval-augmented genera- tion (RAG) techniques. Our approach formu- lates the subject tagging problem as an align- ment task, where records are matched to GND categories based on semantic similarity. We evaluate OntoAligner’s adaptability for sub- ject indexing and analyze its effectiveness in handling multilingual records. Experimental results demonstrate the strengths and limita- tions of this method, highlighting the potential of alignment techniques for improving subject tagging in digital libraries.

metadata.dcterms:abstract: When large language model (LLM) agents are in- creasingly deployed to automate tasks and interact with untrusted external data, prompt injection emerges as a significant security threat. By injecting malicious instructions into the data that LLMs access, an attacker can arbitrarily override the original user task and redirect the agent toward unintended, potentially harmful actions. Existing defenses either require access to model weights (fine-tuning), incur substantial utility loss (detection- based), or demand non-trivial system redesign (system-level). Motivated by this, we propose DataFilter, a test-time model- agnostic defense that removes malicious instructions from the data before it reaches the backend LLM. DataFilter is trained with supervised fine-tuning on simulated injections and leverages both the user’s instruction and the data to selectively strip adversarial content while preserving benign information. Across multiple benchmarks, DataFilter consistently reduces the prompt injection attack success rates to near zero while maintaining the LLMs’ utility. DataFilter delivers strong security, high utility, and plug-and-play deployment, making it a strong practical defense to secure black-box commercial LLMs against prompt injection. Towards Measuring and Quantifying the Comprehensibility of Process Models — The Process Model Comprehension Framework
metadata.dcterms:creator: Winter1*, Michael
Pryss2, Rüdiger
Fink3, Matthias
Reichert1, Manfred
metadata.dcterms:abstract: Process models constitute crucial artifacts in modern information systems and, hence, the proper comprehension of these models is of utmost importance in the utilization of such systems. Generally, process models are considered from two different perspectives: process modelers and readers. Both perspectives share similarities and differences in the comprehension of process models (e.g., diverse experiences when working with process models). The literature proposed many rules and guidelines to ensure a proper comprehension of process models for both perspectives. As a novel contribution in this context, this paper introduces the Process Model Comprehension Framework (PMCF) as a ﬁrst step towards the measurement and quantiﬁcation of the perspectives of process modelers and readers as well as the interaction of both regarding the comprehension of process models. Therefore, the PMCF describes an Evaluation Theory Tree based on the Communication Theory as well as the Conceptual Modeling Quality Framework and considers a total of 96 quality metrics in order to quantify process model comprehension. Furthermore, the PMCF was evaluated in a survey with 131 participants and has been implemented as well as applied successfully in a practical case study including 33 participants. To conclude, the PMCF allows for the identiﬁcation of pitfalls and provides related information about how to assist process modelers as well as readers in order to foster and enable a proper comprehension of process models.

metadata.dcterms:title: Use of tuberculosis interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) in low- and middle-income countries : policy statement
metadata.dcterms:creator: World Health Organization
metadata.dcterms:abstract:
This policy statement provides evidence-based recommendations on the use of commercial interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) for tuberculosis (TB) in low- and middle-income countries, particularly settings with a high TB and/or HIV burden. Based on systematic reviews and GRADE assessment, it evaluates IGRAs for diagnosis of active TB, detection of latent TB infection (LTBI) in children and people living with HIV, screening of health care workers and contacts, outbreak investigations, and prediction of progression to active disease.
The evidence was generally of low or very low quality and did not demonstrate superior performance of IGRAs over the tuberculin skin test (TST). WHO recommends that IGRAs and the TST not be used to diagnose active TB or identify individuals at risk of developing active disease, and that IGRAs not replace the TST for LTBI diagnosis in children, people living with HIV, or contacts. Given comparable performance, greater cost and technical complexity, replacing the TST with IGRAs as a public health intervention in resource-constrained settings is not recommended.

This WHO guidance provides evidence-based recommendations on optimizing health worker roles through task shifting to improve universal access to key maternal and newborn health interventions. Developed in response to health workforce shortages and inequities in access to care, it assesses whether specific interventions can be delivered safely and effectively by different health worker cadres, including lay health workers, auxiliary nurses and nurse midwives, nurses, midwives, associate clinicians, advanced level associate clinicians and non-specialist doctors.
The guidance presents 119 recommendations, ranging from practices recommended for implementation to those requiring targeted monitoring and evaluation, rigorous research, or not recommended. It emphasizes that task shifting should complement efforts to increase skilled care and should aim to expand access while maintaining safety. Implementation should consider health-system capacity and local sociocultural, political and financial conditions, with recommendations adapted through national dialogue and considered as packages of interventions rather than in isolation.

metadata.dcterms:title: WHO guidelines for screening and treatment of precancerous lesions for cervical cancer prevention
metadata.dcterms:creator: World Health Organization
metadata.dcterms:abstract:
These guidelines provide recommendations for screen-and-treat strategies to prevent cervical cancer by detecting and treating precancerous cervical lesions. The screen-and-treat approach bases treatment decisions on screening results, allowing treatment soon or ideally immediately after a positive test, rather than requiring histological confirmation. The guidelines compare strategies using human papillomavirus (HPV) testing, visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA), and cytology, linked to treatment with cryotherapy or loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP). They are intended primarily to support policy-makers, programme managers and other health professionals in selecting appropriate cervical cancer prevention strategies according to available resources and existing programmes.
Nine recommendations are provided. HPV-based screening is generally preferred where feasible, while VIA is suggested where HPV testing is not feasible; cold knife conization is not recommended as part of a screen-and-treat strategy. Recommendations apply to all women, with specific guidance for women living with HIV. Decision-making and implementation flowcharts support adaptation of the recommended strategies to country and regional contexts.

metadata.dcterms:title: Consolidated guidelines on the use of antiretroviral drugs for treating and preventing HIV infection: recommendations for a public health approach
metadata.dcterms:creator: World Health Organization
metadata.dcterms:abstract:
This evidence-based guideline consolidates World Health Organization recommendations on the use of antiretroviral (ARV) drugs for treating and preventing HIV infection, providing a comprehensive public health framework for HIV diagnosis, prevention, treatment, service delivery, and monitoring and evaluation across all age groups and populations. Developed in response to advances in scientific evidence and evolving programmatic needs, the second edition updates the 2013 consolidated guidelines and incorporates new recommendations, including universal eligibility for antiretroviral therapy (ART) regardless of CD4 cell count, expanded use of pre-exposure prophylaxis, and optimized approaches to HIV testing, treatment monitoring and management of coinfections and comorbidities. The guideline also outlines the methods used for guideline development and the principles underpinning a public health approach.
The publication provides evidence-based recommendations on HIV testing services, antiretroviral therapy, prevention interventions, differentiated service delivery models, linkage to care, adherence, decentralization, task sharing, laboratory services and programme monitoring. It emphasizes integrated, people-centred and community-based approaches to improve access to high-quality HIV services, strengthen health systems and support implementation in diverse epidemiological settings. Intended primarily for national HIV programme managers, clinicians, policy-makers and implementing partners, the guideline aims to accelerate progress towards universal access to HIV services and the global goal of ending the HIV epidemic as a major public health threat by 2030.

metadata.dcterms:title: The use of loop-mediated isothermal amplification (TB-LAMP) for the diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis: policy guidance
metadata.dcterms:creator: World Health Organization
metadata.dcterms:abstract:
Tuberculosis remains a major global public health challenge, and the WHO End TB Strategy emphasizes the need for early diagnosis and universal drug-susceptibility testing. This policy guidance presents evidence-based recommendations on the use of the commercial loop-mediated isothermal amplification assay (TB-LAMP) for the diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis. Developed following a systematic review of studies conducted since 2012 and assessment using the GRADE approach, the document evaluates the diagnostic accuracy of TB-LAMP as a replacement for sputum-smear microscopy, as an add-on test after negative smear microscopy, and in comparison with the Xpert MTB/RIF assay, while also assessing the frequency of indeterminate or invalid results.
Based on the available evidence, WHO recommends that TB-LAMP may be used as a replacement for sputum-smear microscopy in adults with signs and symptoms of pulmonary tuberculosis and as a follow-on test when further investigation of smear-negative specimens is required. The guidance emphasizes that these conditional recommendations are based on very low-quality evidence, apply to sputum specimens from patients with suspected pulmonary tuberculosis, and should not replace rapid molecular tests capable of detecting rifampicin resistance. It also highlights the limited evidence for use in people living with HIV, notes the extrapolation of recommendations to children, and provides implementation considerations and priorities for future research.

metadata.dcterms:title: WHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience
metadata.dcterms:creator: World Health Organization
metadata.dcterms:abstract:
This guideline presents the World Health Organization’s evidence-based recommendations on routine antenatal care to support a positive pregnancy experience for pregnant women and adolescent girls. It aims to provide a comprehensive, consolidated framework for antenatal care that complements existing WHO guidance on the management of specific pregnancy-related complications. The recommendations promote a person-centred, rights-based approach that extends beyond the prevention of maternal and perinatal morbidity and mortality to enhance women’s physical, psychological and sociocultural well-being, support healthy pregnancies, and improve the quality and utilization of antenatal care. Intended for policy-makers, programme managers and health professionals, the guideline informs the development of national policies, clinical protocols and service delivery models.
Developed according to the WHO guideline development process, the document draws on systematic reviews and applies the GRADE and GRADE-CERQual approaches together with the DECIDE evidence-to-decision framework. It contains 49 recommendations covering nutritional interventions, maternal and fetal assessment, preventive measures, management of common physiological symptoms, and health system interventions to improve antenatal care utilization and quality. The guideline also introduces the 2016 WHO antenatal care model, recommending a minimum of eight contacts during pregnancy, and emphasizes implementation, dissemination and periodic updating as new evidence becomes available.

metadata.dcterms:title: National health workforce accounts: a handbook
metadata.dcterms:creator: World Health Organization
metadata.dcterms:abstract:
This handbook introduces the National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA), a standardized framework developed by the World Health Organization to strengthen health workforce information systems and support evidence-based workforce planning and policy-making. The publication is intended to assist countries in monitoring and analysing health workforce capacity, distribution, education, labour market dynamics, financing, governance and information systems in the context of universal health coverage and the health-related Sustainable Development Goals. It outlines the rationale for improved health workforce data and highlights the role of harmonized metrics in addressing challenges related to workforce availability, accessibility, performance and retention.
The handbook presents a modular framework comprising 78 core indicators organized across 10 modules covering active workforce stock, education and training, regulation and accreditation, education financing, labour market flows, employment conditions, workforce spending and remuneration, skill mix, governance, and health workforce information systems. For each indicator, it provides definitions, methodological guidance, reporting requirements, data sources and disaggregation options. The publication also describes implementation principles, reporting standards and potential applications of the NHWA, supporting countries in strengthening health workforce monitoring, facilitating international comparability and informing policies aimed at improving health system performance and population access to quality health services.

metadata.dcterms:title: Understanding national health workforce accounts
metadata.dcterms:creator: World Health Organization
metadata.dcterms:abstract:
Understanding National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) is an introductory guidance document developed by the World Health Organization to explain the purpose, policy relevance and structure of the National Health Workforce Accounts framework. The publication outlines how NHWA supports the standardization of health workforce information systems, improves the quality and comparability of data, and strengthens the evidence base for health workforce policy, planning and monitoring. Positioned within the context of universal health coverage, the Sustainable Development Goals, the Global Strategy on Human Resources for Health: Workforce 2030, and related international commitments, the document highlights the importance of reliable workforce information for addressing current and future health system challenges.
The publication describes the benefits of NHWA at national, regional and global levels and presents key policy questions that can be informed through systematic workforce data collection and analysis. It introduces the health labour market framework used by NHWA, emphasizing workforce production, labour market flows, distribution, productivity and regulation. The document also summarizes the development process of the NHWA indicators and explains the modular structure of the framework, which comprises ten modules covering workforce stock, education, labour market dynamics, employment conditions, financing, governance, planning and information systems. Together, these elements provide a foundation for evidence-informed decision-making and strengthened health workforce monitoring.

metadata.dcterms:abstract:
This publication compiles WHO recommendations on maternal health that have been approved by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee into a single, accessible reference for WHO staff, policy-makers, programme managers and health professionals. It brings together current WHO guidance covering the continuum of maternal care during pregnancy, childbirth and the postnatal period, with the dual purpose of facilitating access to recommendations and helping identify areas where further guideline updates are needed. The document indicates newly issued and updated recommendations since 2013 and provides, for each recommendation, its strength, the quality of supporting evidence and the corresponding source guideline.
The compilation addresses interventions to promote, prevent and protect maternal and perinatal health, including antenatal care, prevention and management of pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, peripartum infections, labour and childbirth, postpartum haemorrhage, postnatal care and health promotion, as well as the management of maternal conditions such as HIV infection, malaria and tuberculosis. Developed according to WHO’s guideline development process using the GRADE approach and structured evidence-to-decision frameworks, it presents evidence-informed recommendations intended to support consistent policy development, clinical practice and programme implementation across diverse health-care settings.

metadata.dcterms:title: Classification of digital health interventions v1.0: a shared language to describe the uses of digital technology for health
metadata.dcterms:creator: World Health Organization
metadata.dcterms:abstract:
This publication presents version 1.0 of the World Health Organization’s Classification of Digital Health Interventions (DHIs), a taxonomy developed to provide a shared and standardized language for describing how digital and mobile technologies are used to address health system needs. Intended primarily for public health audiences, the framework supports communication among policymakers, programme planners, implementers, researchers, donors and technology specialists by defining digital health interventions as discrete digital functionalities linked to specific health objectives. The classification was developed to facilitate evidence synthesis, landscape analyses, planning processes and the articulation of digital solutions to identified health system challenges.
The framework organizes digital health interventions into four primary groups according to the main user: clients, health-care providers, health system managers and data services. It links digital interventions to broader health system challenges and to system categories such as electronic medical records, logistics management information systems and telemedicine platforms. Developed through technical consultations, literature review and public feedback, the classification builds on existing mHealth and eHealth frameworks while providing a simplified and practical reference for health programmes. The document is intended to support the design, implementation, evaluation and interoperability of digital health initiatives and will be periodically updated to reflect emerging technologies and evolving practices in digital health.

metadata.dcterms:title: National health workforce accounts: implementation guide
metadata.dcterms:creator: World Health Organization
metadata.dcterms:abstract:
The National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) Implementation Guide provides practical guidance for countries on establishing and sustaining systems to collect, analyse, use and report standardized health workforce data. Developed as a companion document to the NHWA Handbook and in support of the Global Strategy on Human Resources for Health: Workforce 2030, the guide outlines a structured approach to strengthening health workforce information systems and improving the availability, quality and use of human resources for health data. It is intended for policy-makers, programme managers, technical experts and stakeholders involved in health workforce planning, monitoring and governance, and emphasizes collaboration across sectors such as health, education, labour, finance and statistics.
The guide presents an implementation framework organized into three phases—conceptualization, operationalization, and scaling up and sustainability—comprising eight steps that address political commitment, governance arrangements, planning, legal considerations, data compilation and analysis, validation, dissemination, and process review. It describes the roles of national institutions and multistakeholder coordination mechanisms, provides guidance on data quality, reporting and communication processes, and promotes the integration of existing information systems. By supporting the systematic monitoring of health workforce indicators, the guide aims to strengthen evidence-informed decision-making and contribute to health workforce development, universal health coverage and broader national and global health objectives.

metadata.dcterms:title: WHO recommendations on home-based records for maternal, newborn and child health
metadata.dcterms:creator: World Health Organization
metadata.dcterms:abstract:
This WHO guideline provides evidence-based recommendations on the use of home-based records for maternal, newborn and child health (MNCH). Home-based records, whether paper or electronic, are household-held documents that complement facility-based records by documenting health services received and supporting continuity of care. Developed through the WHO guideline development process using systematic reviews, GRADE and GRADE-CERQual approaches, the guideline evaluates the effects of home-based records on MNCH outcomes, health service delivery, acceptability, feasibility and equity, addressing an important evidence gap despite their widespread use in at least 163 countries.
The guideline recommends the use of home-based records alongside facility-based records for pregnant women, mothers, newborns and children to improve care-seeking behaviours, household support and male involvement, maternal and child home care practices, infant and child feeding, and communication between health providers and women or caregivers. It concludes that current evidence is insufficient to identify a superior record type, format or design, and advises policy-makers to engage stakeholders when determining record content and implementation. The publication also discusses implementation considerations, highlights privacy and sustainability issues, identifies research gaps, and outlines priorities for future evidence generation and guideline updates.

metadata.dcterms:title: WHO guideline: recommendations on digital interventions for health system strengthening
metadata.dcterms:creator: World Health Organization
metadata.dcterms:abstract:
This WHO guideline provides evidence-based recommendations on the use of digital interventions to strengthen health systems and support progress towards universal health coverage (UHC). Developed in response to the growing adoption of digital technologies and the 2018 World Health Assembly resolution on digital health, it addresses the need for rigorous evaluation of digital health interventions to ensure that investments are informed by evidence of their benefits, harms, acceptability, feasibility, resource implications and equity considerations. The guideline emphasizes that digital technologies should complement, rather than replace, the fundamental components of well-functioning health systems.
The recommendations focus on a prioritized set of digital health interventions accessible at a minimum through mobile devices, including birth and death notification, stock notification and commodity management, client-to-provider and provider-to-provider telemedicine, targeted client communication, digital tracking of clients’ health status and services, health worker decision support, and digital learning for health workers. The guideline also outlines implementation considerations, identifies research gaps, and supports ministries of health, public health practitioners, development partners and other stakeholders in making evidence-based decisions on the adoption, scale-up and institutionalization of effective digital health interventions.

metadata.dcterms:title: Consolidated guidelines on HIV testing services, 2019
metadata.dcterms:creator: World Health Organization
metadata.dcterms:abstract:
This guideline provides comprehensive, evidence-based recommendations to support countries in delivering high-quality, person-centred HIV testing services (HTS) across diverse populations and settings. Updating and consolidating previous WHO guidance issued in 2015 and 2016, it incorporates new evidence on HIV self-testing, social network-based HIV testing approaches, western blotting, and strategic service delivery to strengthen progress towards global HIV targets. Developed using the GRADE methodology and informed by systematic reviews, modelling studies and expert consultation, the guideline aims to improve the effectiveness, efficiency and quality of HIV testing while promoting timely linkage to prevention, treatment and care.
The publication addresses the full continuum of HIV testing services, including demand creation, pre- and post-test services, facility- and community-based testing, implementation considerations for priority populations, strategic planning, diagnostic testing strategies, quality assurance and programme monitoring. It provides updated recommendations on HIV self-testing, provider-assisted referral, social network-based approaches and the use of dual HIV/syphilis rapid diagnostic tests, while emphasizing the WHO 5Cs of HIV testing services: consent, confidentiality, counselling, correct results and connection. Intended for policy-makers, national programme managers, health-care providers and implementing partners, the guideline supports the expansion of equitable, evidence-informed HIV testing services to improve diagnosis and strengthen national HIV responses.

metadata.dcterms:title: WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis: module 1: prevention: tuberculosis preventive treatment
metadata.dcterms:creator: World Health Organization
metadata.dcterms:abstract:
This guideline provides updated WHO recommendations for the programmatic management of tuberculosis preventive treatment (TPT) as part of the WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis. It focuses on the prevention of active tuberculosis among people at increased risk of disease progression, particularly people living with HIV, household contacts of patients with tuberculosis and other vulnerable population groups. The document incorporates new evidence on shorter rifamycin-containing preventive treatment regimens and updates previous WHO guidance to improve the clarity, consistency and global applicability of recommendations.
Developed in accordance with WHO Guideline Review Committee requirements, the publication presents 18 evidence-based recommendations covering the identification of populations eligible for preventive treatment, exclusion of active tuberculosis, testing for latent tuberculosis infection, recommended preventive treatment regimens, monitoring and evaluation, and implementation considerations. Recommendations were formulated using the GRADE approach, taking into account the certainty of evidence, effectiveness, safety, values and preferences, equity, resource implications, acceptability and feasibility. The guideline is intended to support national policy-makers, programme managers and health-care providers in strengthening tuberculosis prevention and advancing implementation of the WHO End TB Strategy.

metadata.dcterms:title: WHO operational handbook on tuberculosis: module 1: prevention: tuberculosis preventive treatment
metadata.dcterms:creator: World Health Organization
metadata.dcterms:abstract:
This operational handbook provides practical guidance for the programmatic management and scale-up of tuberculosis preventive treatment (TPT) in line with WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis. The publication addresses the global burden of tuberculosis infection and the need to expand preventive interventions among populations at high risk of developing TB disease, particularly people living with HIV, household contacts of TB patients and other vulnerable groups. It supports implementation of commitments made at the United Nations High-Level Meeting on Tuberculosis and outlines strategies to strengthen national responses through integrated, people-centred approaches.
The handbook describes the cascade of care for TPT, including identification of target populations, exclusion of active TB disease, testing for TB infection, treatment options, management of adverse events, adherence support, monitoring and evaluation, and ethical considerations. It also provides operational guidance for contact investigation, integration of preventive services with active TB case finding and HIV services, health system strengthening, and resource mobilization. Practical implementation tools, policy considerations and monitoring indicators are included to assist national TB programmes, policy-makers and health-care providers in adapting and scaling up TPT services in diverse epidemiological and health system settings.

metadata.dcterms:title: Consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery and monitoring: recommendations for a public health approach
metadata.dcterms:creator: World Health Organization
metadata.dcterms:abstract:
These consolidated guidelines provide comprehensive, evidence-based recommendations for HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery and programme monitoring across the continuum of HIV care. Updating the 2016 WHO consolidated guidelines, this edition integrates guidance issued between 2016 and 2021 and reflects major advances in clinical practice, diagnostics and service delivery. Developed using the GRADE approach and informed by expert consultation and country experience, the guidelines aim to support countries in implementing high-quality, person-centred HIV services while advancing universal health coverage and progress towards ending AIDS as a public health threat by 2030.
The publication addresses HIV testing strategies, prevention interventions, antiretroviral therapy, management of advanced HIV disease, care for common coinfections and comorbidities, differentiated service delivery, procurement, laboratory services and programme monitoring. It incorporates updated recommendations on HIV self-testing, pre-exposure and post-exposure prophylaxis, dolutegravir-based treatment, rapid antiretroviral therapy initiation, viral load monitoring and community-based models of care. Intended primarily for national HIV programme managers, policy-makers and health-care providers, the guidelines also serve as a resource for technical partners, community organizations and people living with HIV to support the implementation of effective, equitable and people-centred HIV programmes.

metadata.dcterms:title: Contingency fund for emergencies: 2020 annual report
metadata.dcterms:creator: World Health Organization
metadata.dcterms:abstract:
This annual report presents an overview of the activities, financing and operational impact of the World Health Organization’s Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE) in 2020. The publication describes how the CFE enabled WHO to respond rapidly to 14 emergencies in 13 countries and to support the global response to COVID-19 through the release of nearly US$ 44 million. It outlines the Fund’s role in supporting outbreak control, emergency health operations, supply chain management, surveillance, vaccination activities, procurement of essential medical supplies and continuity of health services during infectious disease outbreaks, humanitarian crises, natural disasters and technological emergencies.
The report highlights WHO-supported responses to the COVID-19 pandemic, Ebola outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the Beirut port explosion, Tropical Cyclone Harold in Vanuatu and the humanitarian crisis in north-eastern Syria. It also examines funding allocations, reimbursement mechanisms, donor contributions and accountability arrangements governing the CFE. Through operational examples and financial analysis, the publication demonstrates the importance of rapid, flexible and predictable financing for strengthening emergency preparedness and enabling timely public health action in complex and evolving emergencies.
